transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

What finally got me here is my concentration has become unreliable. I’ll be reviewing a chart at the clinic, or working on a watercolor wash, and realize I’ve read the same line three times because my mind has wandered to everything that could go wrong.
How long have you been noticing this trouble concentrating and the worried thoughts that go along with it—days, weeks, or months?
It’s been about a year and three months now, since I started the formal retirement process.

Is your worry mainly focused on the retirement and what comes with it, or do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different things—health, finances, family, work—even unrelated to retirement?

It’s not just the retirement itself. My mind keeps going over all kinds of things—whether my old patients are being properly looked after, whether the practice handoff is financially sound, whether I’ll be useless once I’m fully retired. Even I can tell it’s more worry than the situations probably warrant.
Along with the worry and trouble concentrating, have you noticed things like feeling restless or on edge, muscle tension, tiring easily, or trouble sleeping?

I do feel worn out by midafternoon, more than I used to. A nap or a quiet morning doesn’t really straighten it out, and things like weeding the garden or standing at my easel feel heavier than they should.
Over this past year, have you noticed feeling persistently sad, down, or losing interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, like painting or gardening?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed a persistent low mood, exactly.
Do you often feel restless, keyed up, or on edge, like you can't sit still or relax?
I’m not sure I’d say I can’t sit still. I do have a hard time really relaxing sometimes, but I haven’t paid much attention to whether I seem restless.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep—trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up feeling unrested?

Most nights, I’m tired when I go to bed, but once the house gets quiet my mind starts going over patient transfers and money details. Then even if I do fall asleep, I’m often awake around four or five, and it feels like I never really settled into sleep.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with excessive, difficult-to-control worry spanning multiple domains (patient welfare, finances, self-worth) persisting for over a year, well beyond the retirement stressor itself. Associated symptoms include difficulty concentrating, easy fatigability, subjective muscle/physical heaviness, difficulty relaxing, and non-restorative sleep with early morning awakening tied to ruminative worry. No persistent depressed mood or anhedonia was endorsed, arguing against a depressive disorder, and while the retirement transition is a clear psychosocial stressor, the worry has generalized beyond this single issue and exceeds expected adjustment reactions, arguing against adjustment disorder. This constellation and duration meet criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder.
